Rabbi Yitzchak Arama (the Ba'al ha-Akedah): His Work, His Torah Teaching and His Place in the Exegetical Revolution of Late Spanish Jewry
A Guide to the Topic of the Source
This article surveys the figure and work of Rabbi Yitzchak Arama, one of the great thinkers of 15th-century Spanish Jewry, focusing on his foundational work "Akedat Yitzchak". The text shows how Arama developed an innovative three-stage homiletical method, intended to provide an intellectual and polemical response to the influences of Christianity and of the radical Aristotelian philosophy of his time. Through a bold synthesis of rationalist thought, biblical exegesis and early kabbalistic sources such as the Zohar, he sought to establish resilience of faith for the educated elite on the eve of the expulsion. Ultimately, the article stresses that his work was not merely literary, but served as a cultural and leadership bridge that enabled the communities of the exiles to preserve their spiritual identity in an age of momentous historical upheavals.
Rabbi Yitzchak Arama (the Ba'al ha-Akedah): His Work, His Torah Teaching and His Place in the Exegetical Revolution of Late Spanish Jewry
Part One: Historical Context and Biography (The Rabbi's Work)
I. Introduction: Defining the 'Ba'al ha-Akedah' and the Chronological and Geographical Framework
Rabbi Yitzchak Arama, known in the history of Jewish thought chiefly by the epithet "Ba'al ha-Akedah" ("the Author of the Akedah") after his central work, Akedat Yitzchak, was a key figure active in Spain during the 15th century.[1] This period, sometimes called "the decline of Jewish Spain", was marked by deep religious and social crises, which reached their climax in the expulsion from Spain in 1492. Arama's life, which began in Zamora, Spain, in 1420 (5180), and ended in Naples, Italy, in 1494 (5254), spans 74 years of historical upheaval.[1]
The chronology of his life, which ended only two years after the expulsion, makes his work and writings a philosophical-historical document of great weight. He was not merely a witness to the catastrophe, but acted within the processes that led to it. As a biblical commentator, rabbi and head of a yeshiva, he played a central role in shaping the intellectual resistance of the Jewish community in Aragon.[1] His great book, Akedat Yitzchak, written intermittently over a period of about four decades, between approximately 1455 and 1495 CE [2], is not merely a collection of homilies; it is an evolving repository of theological defence and internal criticism, adapted to the changing intellectual challenges facing the community amid mounting persecutions and the pressure to assimilate.
II. His Work as Head of a Yeshiva, Educator and Public Leader (The Historical Transition)
Rabbi Yitzchak Arama's work was not confined to merely theoretical writing, but was directly involved in the life of the community and in the struggle for its identity. He was active among the educated Jewish elite of Aragon, which in his time faced a serious threat to the stability of its faith.
A. The Social Context and the Need for a New Method
The urgent problem that Arama confronted stemmed from a practice that had spread among the educated stratum of the Jews of Aragon: attending the sermons of Christian scholars. These scholars expounded biblical passages using philosophical principles, and presented Christian exegesis in the guise of sophisticated intellectualism.[1] This practice endangered the stability of Jewish faith and instilled foreign theological ideas.
B. The Active Response and the Polemical (Agonistic) Aim
Rabbi Yitzchak Arama saw it as a duty to abolish this dangerous practice.[1] His response was at once pedagogical and agonistic (polemical): he himself began to deliver sophisticated sermons, but this time based on pure Jewish thought, as a response and an intellectual "counterweight" to the Christian sermons.[1] These sermons were intended to prove that Jewish thought, drawing on its own sources (such as Midrash, classical Jewish philosophy and Kabbalah), could not only compete with but even surpass the intellectual sophistication of the Christian environment. In this way, he re-established the legitimacy of philosophical engagement within the framework of the synagogue and the Sabbath sermon.
The central idea that shaped his work was that the spiritual leader must provide the educated public with the theological tools to strengthen their identity. The sermons delivered orally were the basis of the written work Akedat Yitzchak, and it was they that shaped its style and its final form.[1] The work, which was his life's enterprise, quickly became a foundational text for the exiles from Spain, since it provided consolation and an intellectual foundation for preserving the glorious Jewish heritage in an age of destruction and exile.[1] The extension of the period of its composition to 40 years, until his death in exile in Naples, attests to a constant adaptation of the work to the changing needs of a community in existential crisis, and strengthens his standing not only as a thinker but also as a spiritual leader who fought for the soul of his community to the last moment.
Part Two: His Central Torah Teaching – 'Akedat Yitzchak'
III. The Structural Method of 'Akedat Yitzchak': A Detailed Analysis of the 105 Gates
Akedat Yitzchak is a comprehensive collection of commentaries and homilies on the Torah and the festivals.[2] The book is built around the Torah portions and the festivals and consists of one hundred and five gates.[1] The foundational and revolutionary structure of the book is a direct result of Arama's pedagogical-polemical aim, as he sought to create a fixed and binding framework for the weekly sermon. Each 'gate' consists of three separate parts, which together serve a synthetic aim:
A. Analysis of the Threefold Method in Each 'Gate'
B. The Significance of the Balancing Structure
This three-part structure was intended for the purpose of "intellectual inoculation". By opening the discussion each week with a systematic philosophical part, Rabbi Yitzchak Arama gave the educated public the theoretical means to understand the foundations of religion rationally. He then embedded and justified those same philosophical ideas within the Jewish homiletical tradition (the Sages and the Zohar).[1] This pedagogical device prevented the intellectual elite from thinking that philosophy stands apart from the Torah, and showed that true wisdom flows from the Jewish sources themselves, thereby strengthening his position against the Christian influences.[1]
IV. The First Gate: The Confrontation with Maimonidean Rationalism
The first part of each gate is the stage on which Rabbi Yitzchak Arama presents his complex theological-philosophical positions. Here he deals with the core topics of Jewish thought, and in particular with the intra-Jewish confrontation over Aristotelianism.
A. Polemic and Inclusion
Rabbi Yitzchak Arama does not reject Jewish philosophy entirely, but seeks to build a philosophical system that is not blindly subordinate to the views of Aristotle, as in his opinion had happened in certain currents of Maimonides' thought. He quotes and cites the views of the great Jewish philosophers, among them Rav Saadia Gaon (Rasag), Rabbi Isaac Israeli, Ibn Gabirol, Rabbi Yehuda Halevi (Rihal), Ibn Ezra, Rabbenu Bachya ibn Paquda, and Maimonides (Rambam).[1]
B. The Use of Internal Criticism
His use of the writings of the critics of Jewish philosophy, such as Rabbi Hasdai Crescas and Rabbi Yosef Albo [1], is of decisive importance. By including these anti-Aristotelian thinkers, Arama shows that he recognises the weak points of the radical rationalist model. He uses internal criticism from within the Jewish tradition to build a theological system more resistant to the crises of faith of his time. Demonstrating the viability of a strong faith required engaging with all the existing intellectual models, and not merely the blind acceptance of one of them.
V. The Second Gate: The Art of Philosophical Homily and the Integration of Sources
The second part of the 'gate' is the heart of Arama's homily, and it is the place where the great pedagogical synthesis takes place. Arama uses a verse from the portion to open a broader philosophical-midrashic discussion.[1]
A. The Integration of Kabbalah into Public Discourse
An especially prominent feature of the sermons in this part is the integration of passages from the Zohar, as well as from the "Midrash ha-Ne'lam" (apparently identified as the Zoharic work "Livnat ha-Sappir" by Rabbi Yosef Angelet).[1] The integration of these kabbalistic sources into a public sermon intended for an educated audience is a radical move. At a time when Kabbalah was still the preserve of narrow circles, and when the Zohar had not yet been printed [1], Arama was among the pioneers in systematically and explicitly integrating kabbalistic mysticism into a philosophical-rational framework aimed at the wider public.
B. The Collapse of the Wall between Philosophy and Kabbalah
This move represents the peak of the trend towards synthesis that characterised Spanish Jewry at the end of the Middle Ages. Arama sees no fundamental contradiction between philosophy (the first part) and Kabbalah (the second part). Instead of rejecting philosophy or placing Kabbalah above it, he uses both as equal and complementary parts within a single theological structure. This is a trend that proved vital for the preservation of religious identity after the expulsion, and it prepared the ground for the development of new kabbalistic-philosophical centres, for example in Safed.
VI. The Third Gate: Explanations and Textual Application
The third and final part of each gate gives the work its practical and exegetical character, by answering concrete questions on the biblical text by way of questions and answers.[1]
The role of this part is to connect the philosophical theory and the abstract homily (parts one and two) with the plain meaning and practical application. Rabbi Yitzchak Arama demonstrates here how complex philosophical principles can serve as powerful tools for understanding the plain meaning and the allusion in the biblical text. He in effect provides proof that the theory he has built is not detached from the sacred text, but is the key to its full understanding, and thereby he concludes the sermon by strengthening the standing of the Torah as the basis of all wisdom.
Part Three: Intellectual Influences and Additional Works
VII. The Network of Intellectual Influences (Internal and External Affinities)
Rabbi Yitzchak Arama acted as a broad-minded intellectual, who critically combined Jewish and general sources alike. His understanding stemmed from deep study of a wide range of classical and religious texts.
A. Classical External Wisdom and Philosophical Criticism
Arama used the writings of classical philosophy, and especially Aristotle's Ethics.[1] However, his use was not one of acceptance, but a critical and purposeful use.
Especially critical is the fact that he quoted extensively from al-Ghazali's "The Intentions of the Philosophers".[1] Al-Ghazali was an important Muslim thinker, whose work served as a religious critique of Aristotelian philosophy and became a source for critical thought. The very fact of Arama's extensive engagement with this text attests to a deliberate use of internal critical sources (from within the philosophical tradition that grew up in the Middle East) in order to strengthen his Jewish theological position. The discovery of a personal copy of "The Intentions of the Philosophers" that was in Arama's possession, including his glosses in the margins, underscores his deep and critical study of the source.[1] This activity demonstrates his intellectual sophistication: he did not merely read philosophy, but chose sources that challenge it in order to build a more stable theological defence.
B. The Synthetic Map of Influences
Rabbi Yitzchak Arama displayed a rare ability to combine and synthesise different currents, while creating a counterweight to the challenges of his time. The following table illustrates the breadth of the intellectual affinities that underlay his teaching:

VIII. 'Chazut Kasha': A Study of the Complementary Philosophical Book
In addition to his masterpiece Akedat Yitzchak, Rabbi Yitzchak Arama also composed the book "Chazut Kasha".[3, 4] This book is defined as a philosophical work.[4]
The existence of these two works makes it possible to understand Arama's literary strategy. Akedat Yitzchak is a philosophical work within the framework of the sermon and of exegesis — an applied and homiletical method aimed at the wider public. By contrast, Chazut Kasha apparently represents Arama's philosophy in its purer, more systematic and more comprehensive form. This dual approach highlights Arama's standing as a comprehensive master: he could confront scholars on the purely philosophical plane (in Chazut Kasha), and at the same time provide the wider public with the homiletical and pedagogical structure needed for spiritual survival (in Akedat Yitzchak).[3, 4]
Part Four: Summary and Conclusions
IX. Historical Assessment and the Legacy of Rabbi Yitzchak Arama
Rabbi Yitzchak Arama stood at a historical and intellectual crossroads. He is considered one of the foremost thinkers of Spain before the expulsion, and his teaching serves as a barometer of the internal and external tensions that threatened Spanish Jewry in the 15th century.
A. His Contribution to Changing the Character of the Sermon and of Exegesis
Arama fundamentally changed the character of the late Spanish sermon. He transformed it from a tool merely of preaching or of teaching halakha into a goal-directed tool of philosophical-pedagogical analysis.[1] The structural method of Akedat Yitzchak ensured theological consistency and enabled the educated stratum to engage with complex topics without becoming detached from the framework of the Torah and the tradition. His attempt to synthesise rationalism, homily and Kabbalah (through a rare integration of the Zohar into public sermons) constituted a solution to the intellectual crisis created by the influence of external philosophy.
B. Akedat Yitzchak as a Tool for Rescuing Intellectual Identity
The work Akedat Yitzchak is historical testimony to an intellectual confrontation with the existential rupture. The initial aim of the work was polemical, since it was intended to counter the practice of listening to philosophical Christian sermons.[1] Arama's success in creating an intellectual Jewish counter-narrative gave the educated community the self-confidence and the theological tools to preserve their identity.
The historical proof of Arama's importance lies in the fact that the work became a foundational text for the exiles from Spain immediately after 1492. The intellectual tools he developed in order to preserve Jewish identity before the expulsion became the spiritual support needed to survive the trauma after it. Thus the work served as a cultural bridge, uniting all the currents of Spanish Jewish thought into a single coherent structure.
C. His Influence on Jewish Thought after the Expulsion
The synthetic method of Rabbi Yitzchak Arama deeply influenced the thinkers who came after him, including Rabbi Isaac Abravanel, who recognised Arama's importance and developed many of his ideas. Arama's work contributed to the transfer of the intellectual trends of Spain to Italy and to the East, and it is one of the cornerstones of the current combining (Maimonidean) rationalism and (Zoharic) Kabbalah that subsequently developed in Safed and in Europe. As a result, Rabbi Yitzchak Arama is not merely the "Ba'al ha-Akedah", but a spiritual architect who supplied the vital intellectual cargo that enabled the expelled Jewry to survive and to rebuild its spiritual world.
